The Saw Sam Sai is a traditional Thai bowed chordophone of the saw family, related to the saw u and saw duang, but with three strings and a bow separate from the body. It is built in three parts, body, neck and bow: the body is a three-lobed coconut shell with goatskin or cowhide stretched over the front, the neck is hardwood or ivory, lacquered, and the bow is horsehair and hardwood. Before playing, gems are often glued to the skin to damp the resonance, and the three silk strings sound so, re and la. It is used above all in the mahori ensemble and in string bands, has served in royal ceremony at least since the Sukhothai period, was popular in the Ayutthaya period, and rose in social standing under Rama II.

其起源有多說，研究者提出波斯、阿拉伯世界、柬埔寨、印尼或泰國等可能；有學者認為源: There are several accounts of its origin: researchers have proposed Persia, the Arab world, Cambodia, Indonesia or Thailand. Some scholars hold that it comes from the Persian kamancheh or the rebab and reached Thailand through trade and cultural contact, and that it is close to the Cambodian tro and the northern Thai salo. It has served in royal ceremony and been part of the mahori ensemble at least since the Sukhothai kingdom; in the seventeenth century La Loubère recorded a small Thai orchestra instrument called the saw, which shows it was popular in the Ayutthaya period, and under Rama II of the Rattanakosin era royal favour refined it and raised its social standing.

Beside the violin the Saw Sam Sai's timbre is softer and more contained, with a desolation particular to the East; it is close to the erhu but finer and more elegant. Its timbre suits the sorrow and poetry of Thai traditional music especially well, and it is used for solos and in chamber ensembles.

The left hand stops the strings or changes the sounding length to control the pitch, and the right hand sets them vibrating. On a chordophone the vibration of the string is amplified by the soundbox. Keep the bowing even and use the weight of the arm rather than the strength of the wrist.
